content:
Moving this post to a new thread. Here's my take: I think that "it would make a lot of equivalences go away" is something we can only do when we are very confident it comes without loss of generality (like UPred or other things internal to Iris like you mention!). There are many examples of things that behave like Iris (on paper) maps but are non-extensional:

  • BDD's
  • Stochastic process
  • Association matrix graph
  • An inductive type containing a Stdlib map where its extensional quotient does not typecheck
  • Junk-valued data structures

When we lose non-extensional maps, we no longer know a priori that anything which behaves like an Iris (on paper) map has a formalization in Iris-Lean. This means that, to reuse anything, a logic will need to need to do define their own versions of existing Iris constructions:

My● (σ : NonExtType) = ∃σ' : MyExtType, ● σ ∗ ⌜∀ k, σ k ≡ σ' k ⌝
My◯ (σ : NonExtType) = ∃σ' : MyExtType, ◯ σ ∗ ⌜∀ k, σ k ≡ σ' k ⌝
My↦ (k : K) (v : V)  = My◯ (singleton k v)

Some questions:

  • Does such a NonExtType always exist (ie. can the quotient construction fail, such as it does for maps inside inductives)?
  • How much of the API which we already have written will need to be reproduced by each custom non-extensional map resource? At the very least, a construction like above may involve writing custom wrappers around all of like, GhostMap.lean.
  • If we avoid the problem of making non-extensional maps work painlessly inside of Iris, does this just mean that library users will face the same problem? Ie. how hard is it to wrangle the ⌜∀ k, σ k ≡ σ' k ⌝ side condition in the above?

Anyways, I get (firsthand) that it's painful, but I think one lesson I've taken from mathlib is that it's usually worth it for library authors to serve as sin eaters for generality. And I've also been burned by Iris-Rocq de-scoping before. What are you folks' thoughts?

Oh! One other thing. At this point, we have enough core stuff done that I'm in favour of adding ExtensionalPartialMap as a constraint to new lemmas even it's not strictly necessary (to speed up our work/save us some grey hairs). Generalizing that "on demand" is easy.

  • Junk-valued data structures

I understand the generality argument, but is it something that should be solved by the *-PartialMap interface(s)? At least to me, it is unclear if these examples are supposed to be covered by it. For now, PartialMap is something that is used primarily in GhostMap and some internal invariant parts.
Plus, it is already fixed to finite maps in GhostMap, which would allow to reuse only some parts of HeapView and Std/* files for non-extensional examples, while spawning equivalences for the rest of the project.

Markus de Medeiros said:

While it's a bit painful to work with, it's not my primary concern. My concerns is: not having extensionality for maps might prevent us from using a good chunk of automation (grind and simp) in a convenient way, even if/when we have generalized rewriting.

Plus, it is already fixed to finite maps in GhostMap, which would allow to reuse only some parts of HeapView and Std/* files for non-extensional examples, while spawning equivalences for the rest of the project.

I think that GhostMap could go either way, I suppose I am mostly concerned with HeapView (I probably should have used that for my example, since the HeapView lemmas would all need to be duplicated as well, and the projects I'm working on build off of HeapView anyways). In hindsight GhostMap I think could have been lazily generalized (starting with an extensional heap) and if you wanted to specialize GhostMap back to extensional maps now that would be fine by me.

Re. automation: I also think this is completely valid. Based on your judgment, do you think that it would suffice to add on extensional versions of the existing theory? I'm picturing a to_extensional attribute (like to_additive) which turns equivalences into equalities and adds an ExtensionalPartialMap instance.

I'm picturing a to_extensional attribute (like to_additive) which turns equivalences into equalities and adds an ExtensionalPartialMap instance.

Did I understand correctly that this attribute should generate new lemmas with equalities assuming ExtensionalPartialMap? That's hard to tell, I guess it could help defining simp/grind hints. Or all of those can be simply duplicated, similar to _L lemmas in the Rocq version.

Sergei Stepanenko said:

Just so that I understand if the examples above are hypothetical or not. Do you use HeapView and non-extensional maps in your projects? Because I remember you mentioned that in some project you used non-finite maps, but was not sure if they are extensional or not.

For non-finite maps I do have a concrete use case (infinite pre-sampling tapes). For non-extensional maps I did have a concrete use case (lower bound measure space resource) but luckily for me these are extensional in Lean (ofc. if I recall correctly they would be non-extensional in eg. Mathcomp-Analysis, since the values the measure takes on non-measurable sets are junk values). So, while in the short term I could get away with extensional maps, I think the mathcomp-analysis formalization is perfectly reasonable and I do not want to eagerly close this kind of door.

Sergei Stepanenko said:

Did I understand correctly that this attribute should generate new lemmas with equalities assuming ExtensionalPartialMap?

Yeah, or as you mention they could be duplicated. Do you think it's worth trying? I believe this would handle all of the pain points I've seen so far, which have to do with pure rewrites, but I'm wondering if you think this is not going far enough.

Just curious, is the second example using finite maps? Or only extensional, but not finite? Perhaps, being extensional could be included there instead, if it doesn't break anything.

Markus de Medeiros said:

Yeah, or as you mention they could be duplicated. Do you think it's worth trying? I believe this would handle all of the pain points I've seen so far, which have to do with pure rewrites, but I'm wondering if you think this is not going far enough.

I think fixing it to extensional maps at GhostMap would help. IMO it would greatly improve user experience in a long run, when it comes to bigger examples with HeapLang/other languages with more conventional heaps. Perhaps, @Zongyuan Liu has some input of BigOps, and whether or not it would improve user experience working with them. I guess there it should also help to improve automation.

Sergei Stepanenko said:

Just curious, is the second example using finite maps? Or only extensional, but not finite? Perhaps, being extensional could be included there instead, if it doesn't break anything.

The second one is not extensional and it could be finite or infinite (the underlying type is a map out of a subset of the power set, basically). The non-extensionality comes from junk values on sets outside of the subset, which is in principle present even in the finite case (I'm not doing this, but I know of one group who is considering such a model).

Sergei Stepanenko said:

I think fixing it to extensional maps at GhostMap would help. IMO it would greatly improve user experience in a long run

Sounds like we should try! If it helps, that's great, and if not then I'm also happy to talk about other ways to make this work.

I've been an advocate of extensionality since day one :)
I share the concern about automation. I fully support fixing GhostMap extensional first to evaluate the option, and we should fix BigOps if it works well.
I also think we should take the lazy approach from now on.

I have not looked into this situation in detail, but I am in general in favor of extensionality and doing generalizations lazily.

If we specialize GhostMap, should we directly specialize it to ExtTreeMap and only use the PartialMap interface for HeapView?
For BigOp, I guess using the ExtensionalPartialMap interface instead of just using ExtTreeMap might be useful.

My needs are met by replacing GhostMap to be based on Std maps, as well as making extensional (or even fixed) duplicates of the BigOp lemmas. Ie. I'm OK with regressing on GhostMap but generalized BigOps are still useful to me :folded_hands:

Michael Sammler said:

If we specialize GhostMap, should we directly specialize it to ExtTreeMap and only use the PartialMap interface for HeapView?

What do you think of the benefits of using ExtTreeMap?
I'm slightly in favour of continuing using the interface, so that the users only need to know one interface instead of two.

With ExtTreeMap, one can use all the lemmas defined for ExtTreeMap and we don't have to duplicate them for PartialMap. But I can also see that having two interfaces can be confusing. If PartialMap has all the operations a user might need, we can also use that.

Let me summarize the discussion: we need some typeclass that incorporates extensional and finitness in a way that there are no diamonds, and use it starting from GhostMap; and for BigOp lemmas we should have duplicate lemmas assuming this instance. Would it be an acceptable solution for everyone? Probably, for this typeclass we could also provide recommended grind/simp attribute set, so that some map conditions can be solved easily (here it is a bit iffy, because I'm not sure if it's an overkill to provide a blanket attribute set).
This works for my purposes. If it turns out that parts of this are still too onerous, I'm also happy to re-evaluate.

By the way, I appreciate your folks patience/suffering in this process of finding the most general set of definitions such that conventional Iris is nice to use again. Not for nothing, I still consider having HeapView based on a generic API instead of a fixed gmap to be a big step forward (ie. if sacrificing non-extensionality is truly necessary, then we can do it)

Sorry for being annoying about these things :P

Btw, do you have intuition why the example from Mathcomp-Analysis has this approach? Is it because they wanted to have a domain with no subtypes? I.e., does it feel like it was an engineering decision or there's some mathematical reason why it could be better to return junk values?

Not annoying for me :) I'm glad that Iris-Lean is being exercised enough that we can figure out which generalizations make sense to keep!

I know that function hierarchies involving subtypes were at some point an issue with the Mathcomp Analysis hierarchy (I was not able to talk about a subtype as a sub-measure space, though that might have been fixed). It could be an intentional decision to make their hierarchy leading up to measures work better, though I shouldn't speculate.

I'm actually much more surprised that mathlib is able to make measures extensional. Coq-Proba uses a non-extensional junk version, knowing about the development of that library I think it's just for simplicity. I believe Coquelicot is extensional, but if I read their paper right it's because they only store the generators of a measure and can't express a general measure itself. FormalML uses a function out of the subtype of measurable sets which is extensional (barring propext) but they don't use a substantial hierarchy either. All to say: do I think it's a difficult engineering decision!
